evals.prompt: Write a competitive comparison brief on Seismic vs Highspot. Seed URLs: https://seismic.com/platform/, https://www.highspot.com/product/. This is for our product team to understand the capability differences before a strategy session.
evals.expected_output: A competitive comparison brief with Bottom Line (2-4 sentences, strategic insight), Executive Summary (4-6 bullets covering what each product is optimized for, where each wins, biggest strategic implication with signal type, and recommendation), and all 7 numbered sections. Section 1 frames what these products are actually competing on (e.g., content governance + AI recommendations vs. guided selling + rep coaching). Section 2 includes a side-by-side comparison table with decision-relevant rows for content enablement. Section 3 names each product's major capability surfaces explicitly as distinct items — not collapsed into 'content enablement' or 'sales readiness.' Section 4 concretely differentiates the workflow each product drives. Section 5 gives specific conditions where each wins. Section 6 includes a strategic implication with signal type language. Section 7 is a direct recommendation. Sources section is populated. The brief is formatted cleanly — short paragraphs, bullets, readable whitespace — not dense prose.

assertions.name: required_brief_structure_present
assertions.description: The brief contains: Bottom Line, Executive Summary, Section 1 (What These Products Are Really Competing On), Section 2 (Side-by-Side Product Comparison table), Section 3 (Capability Breakdown), Section 4 (Workflow Difference), Section 5 (Where Each Wins), Section 6 (Strategic Implication), Section 7 (Recommendation / Takeaway), and Sources.

assertions.name: bottom_line_present
assertions.description: A Bottom Line section is present before the Executive Summary, 2-4 sentences, leads with the core strategic insight rather than summarizing what the brief contains.

assertions.name: executive_summary_present
assertions.description: An Executive Summary of 4-6 bullets is present. It explicitly states what each product is primarily optimized for, where each clearly wins, the biggest strategic implication (with signal type noted), and a recommendation.

assertions.name: comparison_table_present
assertions.description: Section 2 contains a comparison table with at least 7 rows covering decision-relevant dimensions for both Seismic and Highspot as columns.

assertions.name: fact_vs_inference_separation
assertions.description: Architectural claims in Sections 2 and 3 distinguish between what is documented (cited or from official sources) and what is inferred from product behavior or marketing. Inferred claims use appropriately hedged language ('appears to,' 'based on documented behavior,' 'suggests') rather than stating them as verified facts.

assertions.name: no_overclaimed_internal_architecture
assertions.description: The brief does not state internal implementation details — such as exact AI model identities, specific data pipeline sequences, exact API field names, or internal routing logic — as verified facts without cited sources. Where such details are not publicly documented, the report uses 'Proprietary / Not Publicly Disclosed' or explicitly frames the claim as inferred.

assertions.name: capability_breakdown_explicit
assertions.description: Section 3 names each product's major capability surfaces as distinct, explicit items — not collapsed into category labels like 'content enablement platform' or 'sales readiness tool.' A reader finishing Section 3 should be able to list 4+ distinct capability surfaces for each product.

assertions.name: clean_internal_brief_formatting
assertions.description: The brief uses short paragraphs, bullets where useful, and readable whitespace. No section contains a dense wall of text. The document could be shared internally with a PM or product leadership team and read quickly. It does not read like raw research notes.

assertions.name: signal_type_in_strategic_implication
assertions.description: Section 6 applies signal type language (Shipped, Announced, Signal-based, or Strategic Interpretation) to at least one near-term implication or threat claim. Strategic interpretations are not presented as confirmed facts.

evals.prompt: Write a competitive comparison brief on PathFactory ChatFactory vs Qualified Piper. Seed URLs: https://www.pathfactory.com/platform/chatfactory/, https://www.qualified.com/platform, https://www.qualified.com/. I need this for a PM strategy session — both products are AI agent platforms and I need to understand how their operating models actually differ.
evals.expected_output: A competitive comparison brief that explicitly treats both products as agent-based and preserves their operating capability models. Bottom Line and Executive Summary are present. Section 1 frames the real comparison: buyer self-education vs. pipeline conversion, or content-native AI vs. agentic SDR. Section 2 includes a table with agent-relevant dimensions (autonomy level, channels covered, CRM relationship, workflow orientation). Section 3 is the critical test: both ChatFactory and Piper must have their core capability surfaces named explicitly as distinct items — not collapsed into 'conversion' or 'pipeline.' For Piper specifically: web chat, autonomous email, meeting scheduling, offers, and agentic nurture should each appear as named capability surfaces with an explanation of how they connect into an operating loop and where humans remain in the loop. For ChatFactory: content RAG, conversational Q&A, lead capture, content recommendations, AI Actions, and topic cards should each be named. Section 4 concretely contrasts the two buyer journey workflows. Section 5 gives specific conditions for each. Section 6 addresses the M&A context (Salesforce acquisition of Qualified, Kaltura acquisition of PathFactory) with appropriate signal types. Section 7 ends with a direct recommendation.

A reader finishing Section 3 should know exactly what each agent does and where it stops.
